newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Springroll aims at top Asia entertainment deals.
newsitem.headline: Springroll aims at top Asia entertainment deals.

text.p: Jimmy Wee dreams of becoming a top dealmaker and hopes his newly formed Singapore company, Springroll Creative Entertainment Agency, will make him an entertainment mover and shaker in Asia.

"Asia -- the whole market is booming. I feel there are a lot of opportunities in the entertainment industry. A lot of class lounges need entertainers. The government in each country wants to promote the arts. All these need somebody to coordinate, to be the matchmaker, the middleman, the broker," said 47-year-old Wee.
Wee set up his Singapore $1.0 million (US$0.7 million) company seven months ago with the blessing of his present employer, Japan's CD and video distributor Pony Canyon.
Pony Canyon presently has a 75 percent stake in Springroll.

Wee -- with over 20 years' experience in the music industry that includes work for EMI and Warner Music, previously WEA Record -- said he hoped his company would be profitable in about two years' time.
The name Springroll was inspired by a much-loved Asian snack which is rolled up with different ingredients.
Wee saw his company as "a small infrastructure or net" on standby to grab the "fish" when they come in.

The opportunities have begun to stream in. Springroll has been asked to source a company to stage a French play starring actor Alain Delon in Asia. At home, Springroll has invested in a Singapore-made film, "12 Storeys", and is working on its music score.
Springroll has released three albums of Singapore rock and pop music, two of which have been licensed to recording company BMG.
Another five recordings of Singapore and Malaysian artists have been completed and are waiting to be released.
The fashionably bespectacled Wee is known for championing the local music scene and through Springroll, has opened another avenue for local talents to be heard.
Through its label "Cheapskate", young bands can release their music on low budgets of below S$15,000.

Cheapskate recently released a compilation of local bands in an album called "Flush After Use". Playing on Singapore's obsession with cleanliness, Springroll promoted the album by pasting "Flush After Use" stickers in toilets.
Springroll is talking to British company Mute Records about representing their artists in Asia, Wee said.
It sources products for Pony Canyon and other recording companies and receives a royalty as a licensor. Springroll is keen to take on movie, TV and book deals as well.
"You never shoo people away. You never know the next person who walks in could be your next superstar," Wee said.
"Entertainment is a risky business. It's like a jackpot machine, there's no scientific machine to gauge for you whether you are going to get a hit.
"You have to make a decision and say OK, I think I'm going to take a bet on this guy. I feel he is a great talent, I'll take the risk," he said.

Springroll would like to stage a pop festival in Singapore similar to the Montreal Pop Festival. Wee said it was discussing such a plan with a couple of Singapore organisations and if all went well, it could take off this year.

Since Springroll's birth, others in the region have hatched companies with similar ideas, Wee said. Despite potential competition, he is seeking to set up a network with them and may take a small stake or offer his services as a consultant.
